summary: This document reorganizes the IANA registries for BGP Extended Communities type and sub-type values, including the IPv6-Address-Specific form. The aim is to remove interdependencies among the registries so IANA can more easily tell which code points are available.

plainLanguage.summary: Tag lists were tangled together. This untangles them so the people who hand out tag numbers can see which ones are free.

questions: how are bgp extended community types allocated
what is the difference between transitive and non-transitive extended communities
how to request a bgp extended community code point
subtitle: How IANA's BGP Extended Communities code point registries were reorganized so each one stands alone.

tldr.problem: RFC 4360 was not specific about how the IANA registries for Extended Community types and sub-types should be organized, and that caused confusion about which code points were free.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7153 splits them into separate Type registries (transitive and non-transitive), one Sub-Type registry per Type that has sub-types, and two IPv6-Address-Specific registries, and tells requesters what to ask IANA for.
tldr.outcome: The changes are compatible with existing allocations, so protocol implementations are unaffected. They do change the IANA Considerations sections of future specifications. The RFC has been updated by RFC 9184.

today: RFC 7153 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4360 and RFC 5701, and it has been updated by RFC 9184. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with the Old Registries
sections.content:
RFC 4360 defines the BGP Extended Communities attribute, a sequence of eight-octet extended communities. The high-order octet is the Type field. Each Type has a range for transitive types and a range for non-transitive types, and some ranges are split into sub-ranges assigned under "Standards Action", "First Come First Served" or "experimental use" policies.

For Extended Types, the second octet is a Sub-Type and the remaining six octets are the Value. For Regular Types there is no Sub-Type and the Value takes seven octets.

RFC 4360 did not say how the IANA registries for types and sub-types should be organized, which led to confusion. This document reorganizes them to make IANA's code point allocation more straightforward.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tags are two parts and some are one part, and nobody had said how to keep the lists of them. That made it hard to tell which numbers were free.

sections.title: The New Registry Layout
sections.content:
There is one registry for Transitive Extended Community Types and one for Non-transitive Extended Community Types. Each has three ranges, each tied to an allocation policy.

There is also a set of Sub-Type registries. Each covers 0x00-0xFF: values 0x00-0xBF are First Come First Served and 0xC0-0xFF are IETF Review, per RFC 5226. If a Type has Sub-Types, its entry in the Type registry names its Sub-Type registry. Whether a Type has Sub-Types is decided when the Type is first defined and cannot be changed later. A request to create a new Type registry must say whether a Sub-Type registry goes with it.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one big list of kinds of tags, split by whether they travel on. Kinds that have subkinds get their own list, so every list stays small and clear.

sections.title: The Registries Created
sections.content:
IANA replaced the pre-existing registries with the ones in section 5. The Type registries cover the transitive types (ranges 0x00-0x3F First Come First Served, 0x80-0x8F experimental use, 0x90-0xBF Standards Action) and non-transitive types (0x40-0x7F, 0xC0-0xCF, 0xD0-0xFF in the same order of policies).

Sub-Type registries exist for EVPN, the transitive and non-transitive Two-Octet AS-Specific, Four-Octet AS-Specific, IPv4-Address-Specific and Opaque types, and for Generic Transitive Experimental Use. For example, Type 0x00 has Route Target as Sub-Type 0x02 and Route Origin as 0x03. The existing code points keep their meaning; only the references for the registries themselves now point at this document. The "Traffic Action Fields" registry for the Value field was not modified.

The RFC also notes that RFC 5575 calls the "Flow spec traffic-rate" community non-transitive but assigns it a transitive code point, and says fixing that is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Every list was copied over with the same entries. The numbers kept their meanings, so nothing that already worked had to change.

sections.title: IPv6-Address-Specific Communities
sections.content:
RFC 5701 defines the IPv6-Address-Specific Extended Community as a 20-octet quantity whose two high-order octets can be treated as the Type. The first octet is 0x00 for transitive or 0x40 for non-transitive. The second octet was suggested to match the IPv4-Address-Specific Sub-Types, but existing allocations do not always match.

This document therefore modifies RFC 5701 by removing any requirement that the second octet match either IPv4-Address-Specific Sub-Type registry. It asks IANA to create two IPv6-Address-Specific registries, one transitive (0x0000-0x00FF) and one non-transitive (0x4000-0x40FF), both First Come First Served. The transitive one lists Route Target, Route Origin, VRF Route Import and others; the non-transitive one has no entries assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The long-address version of the tag had been told to copy the short-address version's numbering, but it never quite did. Now it simply has its own lists.

sections.title: How to Request a Code Point
sections.content:
A requester should first check whether an existing Type can be used, and if so ask for a code point from its Sub-Type registry. If a new Type is needed, ask IANA for one from the transitive registry, the non-transitive registry or both. The requester states which, and if both should share the same low-order six bits, must ask for that explicitly.

If the new Type has Sub-Types, the request says whether an existing Sub-Type registry can be reused or a new one is needed. A new Sub-Type registry always covers 0x00-0xFF, ideally with the same policy split as above. Where a new community can be several Types, such as transitive or non-transitive, or two-octet or four-octet AS number, the requester must ask for every registry needed, and must explicitly ask for the same value in each registry or in an IPv6-Address-Specific registry if wanted.
sections.plainLanguage: When you want a new tag number, you have to say exactly which lists you want it in. Nobody will guess for you, even if you want the same number in several lists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that no security considerations are raised by this document. It reorganizes registries without changing the usage or semantics of any code point.
sections.plainLanguage: Because only the lists were tidied and no meanings changed, there is nothing new to worry about.
